claim: Etomoxir reduced cell proliferation in patient-derived human prostatic ex vivo tumor explants by an average of 48.4 ± 16.6% (n = 13 patients; p<0.05) at a dose of 100 µM.
source: Consistent with literature reports, etomoxir had weak activity against the LNCaP PCa cell line in vitro, with an IC50 of 170 µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but was considerably potent in the PDEs, in which a dose of 100 µM inhibited cell proliferation by an average of 48.4 ± 16.6% (n = 13 patients; p<0.05) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from patient-derived explants showing quantified proliferation inhibition with statistical significance.

claim: Etomoxir effectively inhibited fatty acid oxidation in patient-derived explants, evidenced by a significant decrease in multiple acylcarnitines in the conditioned medium.
source: Etomoxir effectively inhibited FAO in the tissues, evidenced by a significant decrease in multiple acylcarnitines in the conditioned medium (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of acylcarnitines in conditioned medium from PDEs treated with etomoxir.

claim: DECR1 is robustly overexpressed in prostate cancer tissues compared to normal tissues.
source: The meta-analysis revealed a strikingly consistent deregulation of lipid metabolism genes, including genes involved in FAO (Figure 1C), despite the predicted high inter-individual heterogeneity of patient PCa tissues. We conducted disease-relapse survival analysis using TCGA data for each of the top 20 genes from the meta-analysis. This identified DECR1, a rate-limiting enzyme in the mitochondrial β-oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids, as a robustly overexpressed gene in PCa tissues that is associated with shorter relapse-free survival rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by meta-analysis of four clinical RNA-seq datasets and confirmed in multiple independent datasets.

claim: DECR1 mRNA expression is significantly higher in malignant compared to benign prostate tissues in ten independent expression datasets.
source: Consistently, DECR1 mRNA expression was significantly higher in malignant compared to benign prostate tissues in ten independent expression datasets of PCa tissues versus non-malignant tissues (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of ten independent clinical transcriptomic datasets.

claim: DECR1 expression is associated with increased Gleason score and advanced disease stage.
source: Further analysis of the TCGA data revealed increased DECR1 expression with increased Gleason score or in with advanced disease stage (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA clinical data correlating DECR1 expression with pathological parameters.

claim: DECR1 mRNA expression is associated with shorter relapse-free survival rates and overall survival rates.
source: DECR1 mRNA expression was associated with shorter relapse-free survival rates and overall survival rates (Figure 1H), and in the TCGA dataset, DECR1 amplification was significantly associated with shorter recurrence-free survival rates (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis from multiple clinical datasets including TCGA, Glinsky et al., 2005, GSE21032, and GSE16560.

claim: DECR1 amplification is significantly associated with shorter recurrence-free survival rates in the TCGA dataset.
source: DECR1 mRNA expression was associated with shorter relapse-free survival rates and overall survival rates (Figure 1H), and in the TCGA dataset, DECR1 amplification was significantly associated with shorter recurrence-free survival rates (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic and survival analysis of TCGA data.

claim: DECR1 protein is overexpressed in clinical prostate cancer tissues compared to benign tissues.
source: We confirmed overexpression of DECR1 protein in clinical PCa using two independent proteomic datasets (Figure 2A). We observed overexpression of DECR1 in PCa tissues (n = 8) compared with benign tissues (n = 3) (Figure 2B), and increased expression was evident in high grade versus low grade cancer tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data from two independent datasets and immunohistochemistry validation.

claim: DECR1 expression is markedly increased in hormone-dependent and -independent cancer cell lines compared with non-malignant prostate cell lines.
source: DECR1 expression was markedly increased in a panel of hormone-dependent and -independent cancer cell lines compared with non-malignant PNT1 and PNT2 prostate cell lines (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis of DECR1 protein expression across multiple cell lines.

claim: DECR1 localizes to the mitochondria.
source: Consistent with its function, DECR1 localises to the mitochondria, confirmed using immunocytochemistry and Western blot of nuclear, cytoplasmic and mitochondrial cell fractions (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation experiments.

claim: Androgen (5α-dihydrotestosterone) significantly decreased DECR1 expression in androgen-dependent LNCaP and VCaP cell lines at both mRNA and protein levels.
source: We confirmed that androgen (5α-dihydrotestosterone) significantly decreased DECR1 expression in androgen-dependent LNCaP and VCaP cell lines at both mRNA and protein levels (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR and Western blot data from DHT-treated cells.

claim: Treatment with the androgen antagonist enzalutamide significantly increased DECR1 expression at both mRNA and protein levels in LNCaP and VCaP cells.
source: In contrast to the effect of androgens, AR-targeted therapies increase DECR1 expression. LNCaP and VCaP cell treatment with the androgen antagonist enzalutamide (ENZ) significantly increased DECR1 expression at both mRNA and protein levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR and Western blot data from enzalutamide-treated cells.

claim: LNCaP tumors exhibited increased DECR1 expression in mice treated with enzalutamide or castration, which was enhanced further in mice treated with both enzalutamide and castration.
source: In vivo, LNCaP tumors exhibited increased DECR1 expression in mice treated with ENZ (10 mg/kg) or castration, which was enhanced further in mice treated with both ENZ and castration (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo qRT-PCR data from LNCaP xenograft tumors under different treatment conditions.

claim: Enzalutamide treatment of patient-derived explants significantly increased DECR1 expression.
source: To confirm androgenic regulation of DECR1 in a clinical context, we validated these data using PDEs. ENZ treatment of PDEs significantly increased DECR1 expression whereas, as expected, mRNA levels of the well-characterized AR target genes KLK3 and KLK2 were decreased (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR and IHC data from patient-derived explants treated with enzalutamide.

claim: AR binds directly to the DECR1 promoter in response to DHT treatment in VCaP cells.
source: To determine whether AR directly represses DECR1, we interrogated published chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) sequencing data. In VCaP cells, AR bound strongly to the DECR1 promoter in response to DHT treatment, but not when co-treated with AR antagonists (Figure 3F; GSE55064).
evidence: The claim is supported by published ChIP-seq data from VCaP cells.

claim: AR binding is enriched at the DECR1 promoter in benign and malignant prostate tissues.
source: Moreover, AR binding was enriched at the DECR1 promoter in benign and malignant prostate tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; GSE56288).
evidence: The claim is supported by published ChIP-seq data from clinical prostate tissues.

claim: DHT stimulates AR occupancy at the DECR1 promoter region in LNCaP cells.
source: A site-specific ChIP-qPCR assay revealed DHT-stimulated AR occupancy at this region in LNCaP cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR experimental data from LNCaP cells.

claim: DECR1 is a novel AR-repressed gene.
source: Collectively, these data reveal DECR1 as a novel AR-repressed gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including expression changes with androgen/anti-androgen treatment and ChIP data showing AR binding to DECR1 promoter.

claim: DECR1 knockdown resulted in an increase in linoleic acid levels in LNCaP cells.
source: DECR1 knockdown resulted in an increase in linoleic acid (Figure 4C) as well as an accumulation of 2-trans,4-cis-decadienoylcarnitine (acylcarnitine 10:2; Figure 4D), an intermediate of linoleic acid metabolism, indicating incomplete PUFA β-oxidation.
evidence: The claim is supported by GC QQQ targeted metabolomics data from DECR1 knockdown cells.

claim: DECR1 knockdown resulted in accumulation of 2-trans,4-cis-decadienoylcarnitine (acylcarnitine 10:2), an intermediate of linoleic acid metabolism, indicating incomplete PUFA β-oxidation.
source: DECR1 knockdown resulted in an increase in linoleic acid (Figure 4C) as well as an accumulation of 2-trans,4-cis-decadienoylcarnitine (acylcarnitine 10:2; Figure 4D), an intermediate of linoleic acid metabolism, indicating incomplete PUFA β-oxidation.
evidence: The claim is supported by acylcarnitine measurements in cell lysates and conditioned medium from DECR1 knockdown cells.

claim: LNCaP cells increased ATP levels in response to exogenous linoleic acid supplementation when cultured in glucose-free media containing the lipase inhibitor DEUP.
source: LNCaP cells increased ATP levels in response to exogenous linoleic acid supplementation when cultured in glucose-free media containing the lipase inhibitor diethylumbelliferyl phosphate (DEUP), to prevent the cells from using intracellular FAs (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP quantification assays in LNCaP cells under defined culture conditions.

claim: Cells transfected with DECR1-targeting siRNAs failed to increase ATP levels with linoleic acid supplementation.
source: However, cells transfected with DECR1-targeting siRNAs failed to increase ATP levels with linoleic acid supplementation (Figure 4E), indicating impaired capacity to metabolize PUFAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP quantification assays comparing control and DECR1 knockdown cells supplemented with linoleic acid.

claim: Exogenous linoleic acid stimulated basal oxygen consumption rates, maximal respiration, ATP production, and mitochondrial spare capacity in LNCaP cells.
source: Exogenous linoleic acid stimulated basal oxygen consumption rates (OCR), as a measure of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, and maximal respiration, ATP production, and mitochondrial spare capacity (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) as determined by consecutive cell exposure to respiration chain inhibitors and uncouplers.
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis data from LNCaP cells supplemented with linoleic acid.

claim: DECR1 knockdown prevented the exogenous linoleic acid induction of basal and maximal respiration, ATP production, and mitochondrial spare capacity.
source: Importantly, DECR1 knockdown prevented the exogenous linoleic acid induction of basal and maximal respiration, ATP production, and mitochondrial spare capacity (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis comparing control and DECR1 knockdown cells with linoleic acid supplementation.

claim: DECR1 knockdown has no impact on mitochondrial metabolism of the saturated fatty acid palmitate.
source: In contrast, DECR1 knockdown has no impact on mitochondrial metabolism of the saturated FA, palmitate (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis of DECR1 knockdown cells supplemented with palmitic acid.

claim: DECR1 knockdown increased glycolysis, as determined by extracellular acidification rate (ECAR).
source: Further, DECR1 knockdown increased glycolysis, as determined by ECAR (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), as well as decreased glucose and fructose concentrations (Figure 4I), to sustain TCA cycle intermediate levels (Figure 4J) as a consequence of disruption of PUFA β-oxidation.
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis measuring ECAR in DECR1 knockdown cells.

claim: DECR1 knockdown decreased glucose and fructose concentrations in LNCaP cells.
source: Further, DECR1 knockdown increased glycolysis, as determined by ECAR (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), as well as decreased glucose and fructose concentrations (Figure 4I), to sustain TCA cycle intermediate levels (Figure 4J) as a consequence of disruption of PUFA β-oxidation.
evidence: The claim is supported by GC QQQ targeted metabolomics data from DECR1 knockdown cells.

claim: DECR1 is critical for PUFA metabolism in LNCaP prostate cancer cells.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that DECR1 is critical for PUFA metabolism in LNCaP PCa cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple metabolic assays showing selective impairment of PUFA oxidation upon DECR1 knockdown.

claim: DECR1 downregulation had no effect on the non-malignant prostate cell line PNT1.
source: While there was no effect of DECR1 downregulation on the non-malignant prostate cell line PNT1, a significant attenuation of PCa proliferation and induction of cell death was observed in a panel of PCa lines (Figure 5A), comprising androgen-dependent (VCaP and LNCaP), CRPC (22RV1 and V16D) and acquired ENZ-resistant cells (MR49F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability and cell death assays in PNT1 cells following DECR1 knockdown.

claim: DECR1 downregulation significantly attenuated prostate cancer cell proliferation and induced cell death in a panel of PCa lines comprising androgen-dependent, CRPC, and acquired ENZ-resistant cells.
source: While there was no effect of DECR1 downregulation on the non-malignant prostate cell line PNT1, a significant attenuation of PCa proliferation and induction of cell death was observed in a panel of PCa lines (Figure 5A), comprising androgen-dependent (VCaP and LNCaP), CRPC (22RV1 and V16D) and acquired ENZ-resistant cells (MR49F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability and cell death assays across multiple prostate cancer cell lines.

claim: The effect of DECR1 knockdown on prostate cancer cell viability was lost when cells were cultured in lipid-depleted media.
source: Notably, this effect on PCa cell viability was lost when cells were cultured in lipid-depleted media (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the observed effect is due to interference with FA metabolism.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assays comparing DECR1 knockdown effects in full serum versus lipid-depleted media.

claim: Stable DECR1 knockdown attenuated LNCaP cell viability and induced cell death.
source: Likewise, stable DECR1 knockdown using a short hairpin vector attenuated LNCaP cell line viability and induced cell death (Figure 5B)
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability and cell death assays in stable DECR1 knockdown LNCaP cells.

claim: Stable DECR1 overexpression significantly enhanced LNCaP cell viability and colony formation ability.
source: In contrast, stable DECR1 overexpression significantly enhanced LNCaP cell viability (Figure 5C) and colony formation ability (Figure 5D), while stable DECR1 knockdown markedly decreased colony formation (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assays and colony formation assays in stable DECR1-overexpressing LNCaP cells.

claim: Stable DECR1 knockdown markedly decreased colony formation in LNCaP cells.
source: In contrast, stable DECR1 overexpression significantly enhanced LNCaP cell viability (Figure 5C) and colony formation ability (Figure 5D), while stable DECR1 knockdown markedly decreased colony formation (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assays in stable DECR1 knockdown LNCaP cells.

claim: DECR1 knockdown decreased LNCaP growth in 3D spheroids.
source: DECR1 knockdown also decreased LNCaP growth in 3D spheroids (Figure 5F), which better mimic in vivo conditions than 2-dimensional cell culture (Duval et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D spheroid growth assays in DECR1 knockdown LNCaP and 22RV1 cells.

claim: DECR1 knockdown reduced LNCaP, 22RV1 and MR49F cell migration by approximately 50%.
source: In addition, DECR1 knockdown reduced LNCaP, 22RV1 and MR49F cell migration by ~50% (Figure 5G) and 22RV1 invasion by ~65% (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell migration assays in multiple prostate cancer cell lines.

claim: DECR1 knockdown reduced 22RV1 invasion by approximately 65%.
source: In addition, DECR1 knockdown reduced LNCaP, 22RV1 and MR49F cell migration by ~50% (Figure 5G) and 22RV1 invasion by ~65% (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell invasion assays in 22RV1 cells.

claim: LNCaP cells stably depleted of DECR1 showed significantly reduced cellular proliferation compared to control cells in subcutaneous tumors.
source: In vivo, LNCaP cells stably depleted of DECR1 showed highly variable growth rates in a subcutaneous model (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), but inspection of the resultant tumors revealed significantly reduced cellular proliferation compared to control cells, concomitant with reduced DECR1 expression (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ki67 IHC staining and mRNA expression analysis of subcutaneous LNCaP xenograft tumors.

claim: DECR1 knockdown significantly retarded tumor growth in LNCaP orthotopic xenografts.
source: To study the effect of DECR1 downregulation on PCa in the prostate microenvironment, we undertook a second study using LNCaP orthotopic xenografts. DECR1 knockdown significantly retarded tumor growth (Figure 5K, (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D,E), and significantly inhibited lung metastasis in the orthotopic tumor model (Figure 5L).
evidence: The claim is supported by IVIS imaging and tumor growth measurements in orthotopic LNCaP xenograft models.

claim: DECR1 knockdown significantly inhibited lung metastasis in the orthotopic tumor model.
source: To study the effect of DECR1 downregulation on PCa in the prostate microenvironment, we undertook a second study using LNCaP orthotopic xenografts. DECR1 knockdown significantly retarded tumor growth (Figure 5K, (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D,E), and significantly inhibited lung metastasis in the orthotopic tumor model (Figure 5L).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo lung imaging and luminescence measurements in orthotopic xenograft models.

claim: DECR1 knockdown resulted in inhibition of PUFA β-oxidation and led to accumulation of PUFAs in phospholipids.
source: DECR1 knockdown resulted in inhibition of PUFA β-oxidation and led to accumulation of PUFAs in phospholipids (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomic analysis of DECR1 knockdown cells supplemented with linoleic acid.

claim: Inspection of the phospholipid profile revealed accumulation of PUFAs in the PC, PI and PS classes following DECR1 knockdown.
source: Inspection of the phospholipid profile revealed accumulation of PUFAs in the PC, PI and PS classes (Figure 6B) with no impact on total saturated or MUFA phospholipids (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomic analysis showing specific phospholipid class changes in DECR1 knockdown cells.

claim: DECR1 knockdown increased levels of malondialdehyde, a marker of lipid peroxidation.
source: DECR1 knockdown increased levels of malondialdehyde, a marker of lipid peroxidation (Gaweł et al., 2004; Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot detection of malondialdehyde in DECR1 knockdown cells.

claim: DECR1 overexpression markedly decreased cellular malondialdehyde levels.
source: In contrast, DECR1 overexpression markedly decreased cellular malondialdehyde levels (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot detection of malondialdehyde in DECR1-overexpressing cells.

claim: DECR1 knockdown enhanced mitochondrial oxidative stress measured using MitoSOX.
source: We observed enhanced mitochondrial oxidative stress measured using MitoSOX, a mitochondrial superoxide indicator (Figure 6D), in response to DECR1 knockdown.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry measurements of MitoSOX fluorescence in DECR1 knockdown cells.

claim: DECR1 knockdown resulted in significant accumulation of phospholipid hydroperoxides, a hallmark of ferroptosis.
source: Moreover, DECR1 knockdown resulted in significant accumulation of phospholipid hydroperoxides, a hallmark of ferroptosis (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by BODIPY-C11 staining and fluorescence imaging of DECR1 knockdown cells.

claim: DECR1 overexpression significantly decreased mitochondrial oxidative stress under basal conditions.
source: In contrast, DECR1 overexpression significantly decreased mitochondrial oxidative stress under basal (Figure 6F) and linoleic acid-induced conditions (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by MitoSOX measurements in stable DECR1-overexpressing LNCaP cells.

claim: DECR1 overexpression significantly decreased mitochondrial oxidative stress under linoleic acid-induced conditions.
source: In contrast, DECR1 overexpression significantly decreased mitochondrial oxidative stress under basal (Figure 6F) and linoleic acid-induced conditions (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by MitoSOX measurements in stable DECR1-overexpressing LNCaP cells supplemented with linoleic acid.

claim: Treatment with the ferroptosis inhibitors deferoxamine or ferrostatin abolished the effect of DECR1 knockdown on prostate cancer cell death.
source: Cell treatment with the ferroptosis inhibitors, deferoxamine or ferrostatin, abolished the effect of DECR1 knockdown on PCa cell death (Figure 6H–I), while cell treatment with the ferroptosis inducers, erastin, FIN56 or ML210, enhanced the cytotoxic action of DECR1 downregulation (Figure 6J–K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assays in DECR1 knockdown cells treated with ferroptosis inhibitors.

claim: Treatment with the ferroptosis inducers erastin, FIN56 or ML210 enhanced the cytotoxic action of DECR1 downregulation.
source: Cell treatment with the ferroptosis inhibitors, deferoxamine or ferrostatin, abolished the effect of DECR1 knockdown on PCa cell death (Figure 6H–I), while cell treatment with the ferroptosis inducers, erastin, FIN56 or ML210, enhanced the cytotoxic action of DECR1 downregulation (Figure 6J–K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assays in DECR1 knockdown cells treated with ferroptosis inducers.

claim: DECR1 knockdown did not induce apoptosis.
source: Supporting ferroptosis as the cell death mechanism, DECR1 knockdown did not induce apoptosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), and the apoptosis inhibitor ZVAD did not rescue the cells from cell death induced by DECR1 depletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by AnnexinV/7-AAD flow cytometry analysis of DECR1 knockdown cells.

claim: The apoptosis inhibitor ZVAD did not rescue cells from cell death induced by DECR1 depletion.
source: Supporting ferroptosis as the cell death mechanism, DECR1 knockdown did not induce apoptosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), and the apoptosis inhibitor ZVAD did not rescue the cells from cell death induced by DECR1 depletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell death assays in DECR1 knockdown cells treated with the caspase inhibitor ZVAD.

claim: DECR1 expression protects cells from oxidative stress.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that DECR1 expression protect cells from oxidative stress and that DECR1 knockdown-induced cell death is primarily mediated by induction of ferroptosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing that DECR1 overexpression decreases oxidative stress markers and DECR1 knockdown increases them.

claim: DECR1 knockdown-induced cell death is primarily mediated by induction of ferroptosis.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that DECR1 expression protect cells from oxidative stress and that DECR1 knockdown-induced cell death is primarily mediated by induction of ferroptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including lipid peroxidation, phospholipid hydroperoxide accumulation, and rescue by ferroptosis inhibitors.

claim: Fatty acid β-oxidation is the main bioenergetic pathway in human prostate cancer.
source: Fatty acid β-oxidation (FAO) is the main bioenergetic pathway in human prostate cancer (PCa) and a promising novel therapeutic vulnerability.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by literature citations and experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: DECR1 encodes the rate-limiting enzyme for oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids.
source: Here we demonstrate therapeutic efficacy of targeting FAO in clinical prostate tumors cultured ex vivo, and identify DECR1, encoding the rate-limiting enzyme for oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), as robustly overexpressed in PCa tissues and associated with shorter relapse-free survival.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by literature on DECR1 function.

claim: DECR1 is a negatively-regulated androgen receptor target gene.
source: DECR1 is a negatively-regulated androgen receptor (AR) target gene and, therefore, may promote PCa cell survival and resistance to AR targeting therapeutics.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing AR binding to DECR1 promoter and inverse regulation by androgens/anti-androgens.

claim: DECR1 may promote prostate cancer cell survival and resistance to AR targeting therapeutics.
source: DECR1 is a negatively-regulated androgen receptor (AR) target gene and, therefore, may promote PCa cell survival and resistance to AR targeting therapeutics.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that DECR1 is upregulated by anti-androgen therapy and its knockdown reduces cell viability.

claim: DECR1 knockdown selectively inhibited β-oxidation of PUFAs.
source: DECR1 knockdown selectively inhibited β-oxidation of PUFAs, inhibited proliferation and migration of PCa cells, including treatment resistant lines, and suppressed tumor cell proliferation and metastasis in mouse xenograft models.
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis and metabolomics data showing selective effects on PUFA but not saturated fatty acid oxidation.

claim: DECR1 knockdown inhibited proliferation and migration of prostate cancer cells, including treatment resistant lines.
source: DECR1 knockdown selectively inhibited β-oxidation of PUFAs, inhibited proliferation and migration of PCa cells, including treatment resistant lines, and suppressed tumor cell proliferation and metastasis in mouse xenograft models.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability, migration, and invasion assays in multiple prostate cancer cell lines including enzalutamide-resistant cells.

claim: DECR1 knockdown suppressed tumor cell proliferation and metastasis in mouse xenograft models.
source: DECR1 knockdown selectively inhibited β-oxidation of PUFAs, inhibited proliferation and migration of PCa cells, including treatment resistant lines, and suppressed tumor cell proliferation and metastasis in mouse xenograft models.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experiments showing reduced Ki67 staining, tumor growth, and lung metastasis in xenograft models.

claim: Targeting of DECR1 caused cellular accumulation of PUFAs.
source: Mechanistically, targeting of DECR1 caused cellular accumulation of PUFAs, enhanced mitochondrial oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, and induced ferroptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomic analysis showing increased PUFA levels in phospholipids following DECR1 knockdown.

claim: Targeting of DECR1 enhanced mitochondrial oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation.
source: Mechanistically, targeting of DECR1 caused cellular accumulation of PUFAs, enhanced mitochondrial oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, and induced ferroptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by MitoSOX measurements, malondialdehyde detection, and BODIPY-C11 staining showing increased oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation.

claim: Targeting of DECR1 induced ferroptosis.
source: Mechanistically, targeting of DECR1 caused cellular accumulation of PUFAs, enhanced mitochondrial oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, and induced ferroptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments with ferroptosis inhibitors and enhancement with ferroptosis inducers.

claim: PUFA oxidation via DECR1 is an unexplored facet of FAO that promotes survival of prostate cancer cells.
source: These findings implicate PUFA oxidation via DECR1 as an unexplored facet of FAO that promotes survival of PCa cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the collective findings showing DECR1's role in PUFA oxidation and its impact on cell survival.

claim: Prostate cancer is the most prevalent male cancer in Western societies.
source: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most prevalent male cancer and the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men in Western societies (Bray et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to epidemiological data.

claim: Prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men in Western societies.
source: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most prevalent male cancer and the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men in Western societies (Bray et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to epidemiological data.

claim: Androgen deprivation therapy has remained the frontline strategy for clinical management of locally-recurrent and/or metastatic prostate cancer since the 1940s.
source: For patients with locally-recurrent and/or metastatic disease, androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) has remained the frontline strategy for clinical management since the 1940s (Huggins and Hodges, 1941), due to the dependence of PCa cells on androgens for growth and survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the seminal work by Huggins and Hodges.

claim: All patients initially responsive to androgen deprivation therapy will ultimately relapse with castration resistant prostate cancer.
source: Although ADT is initially effective in most patients, ultimately all will relapse with castration resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), which remains incurable.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical knowledge about prostate cancer progression.

claim: Castration resistant prostate cancer remains incurable.
source: Although ADT is initially effective in most patients, ultimately all will relapse with castration resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), which remains incurable.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: The failure of androgen deprivation therapy is attributed to the emergence of adaptive survival pathways that reprogram androgen signaling and/or activate alternative tumor survival pathways.
source: The failure of ADT is attributed to the emergence of adaptive survival pathways that reprogram androgen signaling and/or activate alternative tumor survival pathways.
evidence: The claim is based on established understanding of resistance mechanisms in prostate cancer.

claim: Enzalutamide is an AR antagonist approved by the FDA for treatment of castration resistant prostate cancer.
source: Consequently, the development and FDA approval of agents that more effectively target androgen signaling, including enzalutamide (ENZ, Xtandi; an AR antagonist) (Tran et al., 2009; Cai and Balk, 2011; Rodrigues et al., 2014), has expanded the therapeutic options for CRPC.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing enzalutamide's mechanism and approval.

claim: Even advanced androgen signaling targeting approaches cannot durably control tumor growth in castration resistant prostate cancer.
source: Nevertheless, even these approaches cannot durably control tumor growth and there is considerable variability in the nature and duration of responses between different patients (Tran et al., 2009; Scher et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: There is considerable variability in the nature and duration of responses to enzalutamide between different patients.
source: Nevertheless, even these approaches cannot durably control tumor growth and there is considerable variability in the nature and duration of responses between different patients (Tran et al., 2009; Scher et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Prostate cancer is mainly dependent on lipid metabolism for energy production.
source: PCa is mainly dependent on lipid metabolism for energy production (Liu, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The overexpression of genes involved in lipid metabolism is characteristic of prostate cancer at both early and advanced stages.
source: The overexpression of genes involved in lipid metabolism is characteristic of PCa at both early and advanced stages (Wu et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2018; Swinnen et al., 2002; Zadra et al., 2013; Zadra and Loda, 2018; Ettinger et al., 2004; Nomura et al., 2011), while recent proteomic analyses of primary PCa and bone metastases have shown clear associations between levels of lipid metabolic enzymes, PCa initiation and progression (Iglesias-Gato et al., 2016; Iglesias-Gato et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Recent proteomic analyses of primary prostate cancer and bone metastases have shown clear associations between levels of lipid metabolic enzymes, prostate cancer initiation and progression.
source: The overexpression of genes involved in lipid metabolism is characteristic of PCa at both early and advanced stages (Wu et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2018; Swinnen et al., 2002; Zadra et al., 2013; Zadra and Loda, 2018; Ettinger et al., 2004; Nomura et al., 2011), while recent proteomic analyses of primary PCa and bone metastases have shown clear associations between levels of lipid metabolic enzymes, PCa initiation and progression (Iglesias-Gato et al., 2016; Iglesias-Gato et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to proteomic studies.

claim: β-oxidation of fatty acids is upregulated in prostate cancer cells.
source: However, it has become evident in work from our group and others that β-oxidation of FAs, as the ultimate fate of FAs in the energy production cycle, is upregulated in PCa cells, stimulated by a lipid-rich extracellular environment and critical for viability (Liu, 2006; Schlaepfer et al., 2014; Balaban et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work including the authors' own research.

claim: β-oxidation of fatty acids is stimulated by a lipid-rich extracellular environment in prostate cancer cells.
source: However, it has become evident in work from our group and others that β-oxidation of FAs, as the ultimate fate of FAs in the energy production cycle, is upregulated in PCa cells, stimulated by a lipid-rich extracellular environment and critical for viability (Liu, 2006; Schlaepfer et al., 2014; Balaban et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: β-oxidation of fatty acids is critical for viability of prostate cancer cells.
source: However, it has become evident in work from our group and others that β-oxidation of FAs, as the ultimate fate of FAs in the energy production cycle, is upregulated in PCa cells, stimulated by a lipid-rich extracellular environment and critical for viability (Liu, 2006; Schlaepfer et al., 2014; Balaban et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work including the authors' own research.

claim: Etomoxir had weak activity against the LNCaP prostate cancer cell line in vitro, with an IC50 of 170 µM.
source: Consistent with literature reports, etomoxir had weak activity against the LNCaP PCa cell line in vitro, with an IC50 of 170 µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but was considerably potent in the PDEs, in which a dose of 100 µM inhibited cell proliferation by an average of 48.4 ± 16.6% (n = 13 patients; p<0.05) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Human DECR1 deficiency is lethal.
source: Human DECR1 deficiency is lethal, with patients exhibiting hypocarnitinemia, decreased cellular oxygen consumption, increased lactic acidosis, and unusual accumulation of FA intermediates in urine and blood due to incomplete β-oxidation (Roe et al., 1990; Houten et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical case reports.

claim: DECR1-deficient patients exhibit hypocarnitinemia, decreased cellular oxygen consumption, increased lactic acidosis, and unusual accumulation of fatty acid intermediates in urine and blood due to incomplete β-oxidation.
source: Human DECR1 deficiency is lethal, with patients exhibiting hypocarnitinemia, decreased cellular oxygen consumption, increased lactic acidosis, and unusual accumulation of FA intermediates in urine and blood due to incomplete β-oxidation (Roe et al., 1990; Houten et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical case reports.

claim: DECR1-null mice exhibit impaired lipid metabolism, hypoglycemia and activation of ketogenesis, and cold intolerance.
source: DECR1-null mice exhibit impaired lipid metabolism, hypoglycemia and activation of ketogenesis, and cold intolerance (Miinalainen et al., 2009; Mäkelä et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to mouse model studies.

claim: Acylcarnitine accumulation was observed in Decr1-/- mice and DECR1-deficient patients.
source: These results are consistent with previous studies reporting acylcarnitine accumulation in Decr1-/- mice and DECR1-deficient patients (Roe et al., 1990; Miinalainen et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FAO inhibition or impaired mitochondrial function leads to enhanced glucose uptake and glycolysis.
source: We showed that DECR1 knockdown selectively inhibited PUFA catabolism, accompanied by an increase in glycolysis rate, which is also consistent with previous reports of FAO inhibition or impaired mitochondrial function leading to enhanced glucose uptake and glycolysis (Schlaepfer et al., 2015; Houten et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PUFAs are highly susceptible to peroxidation, thereby enhancing free radical generation and accumulation of toxic lipid peroxides.
source: In contrast to MUFAs, PUFAs are highly susceptible to peroxidation, thereby enhancing free radical generation and accumulation of toxic lipid peroxides (Das, 2011; Magtanong et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on lipid chemistry and biology.

claim: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of cell death that is triggered by lipid peroxidation.
source: An important cellular protective response to excess intracellular lipid peroxides is the induction of ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death that is triggered by lipid peroxidation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ferroptosis.

claim: The findings that DECR1 knockdown induces ferroptosis were independently validated in human prostate cancer during revision of this article.
source: These findings are consistent with a mechanism by which DECR1 knockdown-induced cell death is a ferroptosis-mediated process caused by PUFA accumulation, a conclusion that was independently validated in human prostate cancer during revision of this article (Blomme et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an independent study published during manuscript revision.

claim: PUFAs are essential fatty acids that cannot be synthesized in mammals and are only obtained from the diet.
source: PUFAs are essential FAs that cannot be synthesized in mammals and are only obtained from the diet.
evidence: The claim is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Dietary fat promotes prostate cancer progression and disease aggressiveness.
source: Dietary fat not only promotes obesity, but also PCa progression and disease aggressiveness. Several preclinical PCa studies have compared high-fat (or Western-style diets) versus low fat diet and reported that the former promotes AKT and ERK activity, tumor growth, tumor incidence in genetically engineered/transgenic mouse models, tumor progression to CRPC and metastasis (reviewed in Narita et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article summarizing preclinical studies.

claim: High-fat diets promote AKT and ERK activity, tumor growth, tumor incidence, tumor progression to CRPC and metastasis in preclinical prostate cancer models.
source: Several preclinical PCa studies have compared high-fat (or Western-style diets) versus low fat diet and reported that the former promotes AKT and ERK activity, tumor growth, tumor incidence in genetically engineered/transgenic mouse models, tumor progression to CRPC and metastasis (reviewed in Narita et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Clinical case-control studies indicated saturated fat is associated with an increased risk of advanced prostate cancer.
source: Clinical case-control studies indicated saturated fat is associated with an increased risk of advanced PCa (Bairati et al., 1998; Stéfani et al., 2000; Slattery et al., 1990; Whittemore et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple clinical case-control studies.

claim: Omega-3 PUFAs inhibit prostate cancer progression.
source: In contrast to omega-3 PUFAs, which are reported to inhibit PCa progression (Wang et al., 2012), omega-6 PUFAs (Khankari et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2010), and higher omega-6/omega-3 PUFA ratio, increase PCa risk (Williams et al., 2011; Apte et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Omega-6 PUFAs increase prostate cancer risk.
source: In contrast to omega-3 PUFAs, which are reported to inhibit PCa progression (Wang et al., 2012), omega-6 PUFAs (Khankari et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2010), and higher omega-6/omega-3 PUFA ratio, increase PCa risk (Williams et al., 2011; Apte et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Higher omega-6/omega-3 PUFA ratio increases prostate cancer risk.
source: In contrast to omega-3 PUFAs, which are reported to inhibit PCa progression (Wang et al., 2012), omega-6 PUFAs (Khankari et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2010), and higher omega-6/omega-3 PUFA ratio, increase PCa risk (Williams et al., 2011; Apte et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Dietary intervention by decreasing total fat intake and increasing omega-3 PUFAs was found to improve prostate cancer survivorship.
source: Dietary intervention by decreasing total fat intake and increasing omega-3 PUFAs was found to improve PCa survivorship (Epstein et al., 2012; Colli and Colli, 2005; Davies et al., 2011; Ornish et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to dietary intervention studies.

claim: Both omega-6 and omega-3 PUFAs require DECR1 for complete β-oxidation.
source: It is unclear whether there is a preference for n-6 or n-3 PUFA β-oxidation in PCa cells, however both require DECR1 for complete β-oxidation.
evidence: The claim is based on the known biochemical function of DECR1 in the auxiliary pathway for PUFA oxidation.

claim: CPT1 is the rate-limiting step of fatty acid β-oxidation.
source: Although FAO is a complex process that requires the activity of several enzymes, to date the entire focus of drug development strategies has been inhibitors against CPT1, the rate-limiting step of FA β-oxidation.
evidence: The claim is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: CPT1 is responsible for synthesizing fatty acyl-carnitines from fatty acyl-CoAs which are then transported from the cytoplasm into the mitochondria.
source: CPT1 is responsible for synthesizing fatty acyl-carnitines from fatty acyl-CoAs which are then transported from the cytoplasm into the mitochondria by carnitine acylcarnitine translocase for subsequent processing then entry into the β-oxidation pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on established biochemical knowledge of CPT1 function.

claim: CPT1 inhibition would suppress β-oxidation of all long fatty acid species (saturated FA, MUFA and PUFA).
source: Based on our current findings, we propose that DECR1 is an attractive alternative target to CPT1. CPT1 inhibition would suppress β-oxidation of all long FA species (saturated FA, MUFA and PUFA), whilst in contrast DECR1 is specific for PUFA.
evidence: The claim is based on the known function of CPT1 as the entry point for all fatty acids into mitochondrial β-oxidation.

claim: DECR1 is specific for PUFA oxidation.
source: Based on our current findings, we propose that DECR1 is an attractive alternative target to CPT1. CPT1 inhibition would suppress β-oxidation of all long FA species (saturated FA, MUFA and PUFA), whilst in contrast DECR1 is specific for PUFA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing selective inhibition of PUFA but not saturated fatty acid oxidation upon DECR1 knockdown.

claim: Homozygous CPT1 deficiency, of either the liver or muscle isoform, is lethal in mice.
source: Homozygous CPT1 deficiency, of either the liver or muscle isoform, is lethal in mice (Nyman et al., 2005; Ji et al., 2008; Haynie et al., 2014), but Decr1−/− mice are viable, and clinical symptoms arose only after metabolic stress (Miinalainen et al., 2009; Mäkelä et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to mouse genetic studies.

claim: Decr1−/− mice are viable, and clinical symptoms arose only after metabolic stress.
source: Homozygous CPT1 deficiency, of either the liver or muscle isoform, is lethal in mice (Nyman et al., 2005; Ji et al., 2008; Haynie et al., 2014), but Decr1−/− mice are viable, and clinical symptoms arose only after metabolic stress (Miinalainen et al., 2009; Mäkelä et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to mouse genetic studies.

claim: The crystal structure of DECR1 active site has been solved.
source: Of note, the crystal structure of DECR1 active site has been solved (Alphey et al., 2005), and thus developing DECR1 inhibitors is feasible.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a structural biology study.

claim: Developing DECR1 inhibitors is feasible.
source: Of note, the crystal structure of DECR1 active site has been solved (Alphey et al., 2005), and thus developing DECR1 inhibitors is feasible.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the availability of structural information.

claim: The top three cancer types exhibiting increased DECR1 copy gain are hormone-dependent tumors (uterine, breast and prostate).
source: Interestingly, the top three cancer types exhibiting increased DECR1 copy gain were hormone-dependent tumors (uterine, breast and prostate), suggestive of a relationship between DECR1 expression and hormone signaling (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of genomic data from cBioPortal across 28 tumor types.

claim: There is a relationship between DECR1 expression and hormone signaling.
source: Interestingly, the top three cancer types exhibiting increased DECR1 copy gain were hormone-dependent tumors (uterine, breast and prostate), suggestive of a relationship between DECR1 expression and hormone signaling (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that hormone-dependent cancers show high DECR1 copy gain.

claim: DECR1 catalyzes the conversion of either 2-trans,4-cis-dienoyl or 2-trans,4-trans-dienoyl-CoA to 3-trans-enoyl-CoA.
source: DECR1 catalyzes the conversion of either 2-trans,4-cis-dienoyl or 2-trans,4-trans-dienoyl-CoA to 3-trans-enoyl-CoA.
evidence: The claim is based on established biochemical knowledge of DECR1 enzymatic activity.

claim: DECR1 catalyzes the rate limiting step in the auxiliary pathway for polyunsaturated fatty acid oxidation.
source: Given the critical role of DECR1 in PUFA metabolism, we studied the consequences of DECR1 downregulation on β-oxidation of PUFAs in PCa cells. DECR1 knockdown was achieved successfully (>80% downregulation) using two different siRNAs (Figure 4B). DECR1 knockdown resulted in an increase in linoleic acid (Figure 4C) as well as an accumulation of 2-trans,4-cis-decadienoylcarnitine (acylcarnitine 10:2; Figure 4D), an intermediate of linoleic acid metabolism, indicating incomplete PUFA β-oxidation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature and experimental data showing accumulation of PUFA intermediates upon DECR1 knockdown.

claim: Etomoxir inhibited both PUFA and saturated fatty acid oxidation.
source: While DECR1 exhibited selectivity in inhibition of PUFA metabolism, as expected, etomoxir inhibited both PUFA and saturated fatty acids (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis data.

claim: There was no effect of etomoxir treatment on DECR1 expression.
source: There was no effect of ETX treatment on DECR1 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing DECR1 protein levels after etomoxir treatment.

claim: 3D spheroid culture better mimics in vivo conditions than 2-dimensional cell culture.
source: DECR1 knockdown also decreased LNCaP growth in 3D spheroids (Figure 5F), which better mimic in vivo conditions than 2-dimensional cell culture (Duval et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article on 3D culture methods.

claim: Prostate cancer cells commonly select for DECR1 overexpression to enhance ATP production and protect cells from the tumoricidal effects of excess PUFAs.
source: It is therefore possible that PCa cells commonly select for DECR1 overexpression, not only to enhance ATP production to fulfil energy requirements, but also to protect cells from the tumoricidal effects of excess PUFAs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observed overexpression of DECR1 in tumors and its dual role in energy production and protection from lipid peroxidation.
